name: Inspect a running pod
objective: CKAD › Application Observability and Maintenance (15%). Goal: diagnose and fix failing workloads using kubectl logs, describe, and events — CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, Pending (unschedulable), reading container stdout, and a failing readiness probe.

questions.title: Capture a line from container logs
questions.teach:
**`kubectl logs <pod>`** returns whatever the container wrote to **stdout/stderr** — run a pod that prints a line, then read it back. Store the captured value in a ConfigMap with **`kubectl create configmap <name> --from-literal=key=value`**.

**Gotcha:** `logs` only shows stdout/stderr — an app that writes to a file *inside* the container shows nothing.
questions.prompt:
Run a pod `logger` (image `busybox:1.36`) whose command prints the exact line `MARKER=ckad-obs-42` to stdout and then stays running (e.g. `echo MARKER=ckad-obs-42; sleep 3600`). Read it back with `kubectl logs`, then create a ConfigMap `captured` in `ckad-observability` with key `token` set to that value `ckad-obs-42`.

Target: pod `logger` logged `MARKER=ckad-obs-42` AND ConfigMap `captured` has `token=ckad-obs-42`.
questions.hint: `kubectl run logger -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sh -c 'echo MARKER=ckad-obs-42; sleep 3600'`, then `kubectl logs logger -n ckad-observability`, then `kubectl create configmap captured -n ckad-observability --from-literal=token=ckad-obs-42`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run logger -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sh -c 'echo MARKER=ckad-obs-42; sleep 3600'
kubectl logs logger -n ckad-observability   # MARKER=ckad-obs-42
kubectl create configmap captured -n ckad-observability --from-literal=token=ckad-obs-42

verification.description: logger printed the marker AND configmap 'captured' holds token=ckad-obs-42

questions.eli5:
Imagine a little robot in a sealed box. The only way it can talk to the outside world is through a **loudspeaker** on top of the box. Whatever the robot *says out loud* through that speaker, you can hear and write down. That loudspeaker is **stdout/stderr**, and `kubectl logs <pod>` is you pressing your ear to it and reading back everything the robot has said.

So the task is a two-parter. First, build a robot (`logger`, a `busybox` pod) that, the moment it wakes up, shouts one exact sentence — `MARKER=ckad-obs-42` — and then just hums quietly forever (`sleep 3600`) so it stays alive. The `sleep` matters: if the robot shouted and then immediately powered off, the box would be gone and there'd be nothing to read from.

Second, you listen with `kubectl logs`, grab the secret word `ckad-obs-42`, and write it on a sticky note the cluster keeps — a **ConfigMap** called `captured`, with `token=ckad-obs-42`. You make that note with `--from-literal=token=ckad-obs-42`.

**Watch out:**

- **`kubectl logs` only hears the loudspeaker (stdout/stderr).** If the robot writes the word in a notebook *inside* the box (a file in the container), you'll see nothing — logs can't read files.
- **Print the line exactly** — `MARKER=ckad-obs-42`, same spelling and case. The grader checks for it.
- **Keep the pod alive** after it prints (the `sleep 3600`), or it exits and you lose your reading window.
- **`--from-literal` stores the plain value**: the key is `token`, the value is just `ckad-obs-42` — don't accidentally store the whole `MARKER=...` line.
- If the pod crashes and restarts, `kubectl logs` shows the *current* life; add `--previous` to read the one that just died.
questions.deepDive:
## Reading container logs + capturing to a ConfigMap

### Mental model
A container's **logs are whatever it writes to stdout/stderr** (file descriptors 1 and 2). The kubelet captures those streams to disk on the node; `kubectl logs` reads them back. Nothing a process writes to a *file inside the container* ever appears in `kubectl logs`.

```
container stdout/stderr ─▶ kubelet log file on node ─▶ kubectl logs <pod>
```

### Run a pod that prints then stays alive
```bash
kubectl run logger -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 \
  --command -- sh -c 'echo MARKER=ckad-obs-42; sleep 3600'
```
- `--command` makes everything after `--` the container's **command** (overrides the image entrypoint).
- `sh -c '...'` lets you chain `echo` then `sleep` in one process.
- The `sleep 3600` keeps the container `Running` so logs remain readable. Without it the pod would exit (and likely churn in `CrashLoopBackOff`).

### Read the logs back
```bash
kubectl logs logger -n ckad-observability          # MARKER=ckad-obs-42
```

| `kubectl logs` flag | Use |
|---|---|
| `-f` / `--follow` | stream live |
| `--previous` / `-p` | logs from the **last crashed** instance |
| `-c <container>` | pick a container in a multi-container pod |
| `--tail=N` | last N lines |
| `--since=5m` | only recent lines |
| `-l <selector>` | aggregate logs across matching pods |

### Store the captured value in a ConfigMap
```bash
kubectl create configmap captured -n ckad-observability \
  --from-literal=token=ckad-obs-42
```
`--from-literal=key=value` stores one inline key/value pair. Verify:
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-observability get cm captured -o jsonpath='{.data.token}'; echo   # ckad-obs-42
```

| ConfigMap source flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--from-literal=k=v` | inline key/value (repeatable) |
| `--from-file=path` | key = filename, value = file contents |
| `--from-file=k=path` | custom key, value = file contents |
| `--from-env-file=path` | each `KEY=VAL` line becomes a key |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`kubectl logs` shows only stdout/stderr.** An app logging to a file inside the container shows nothing — that's the single most common "why are my logs empty" trap.
- **No `sleep`/long-lived process → the pod exits**, and you may hit `CrashLoopBackOff` with an empty current log; use `--previous` to see what it printed.
- Store the **value**, not the whole line: key `token`, value `ckad-obs-42` (not `MARKER=ckad-obs-42`).
- `--command` is needed so args become the **command**, not container **args** appended to the image's entrypoint.
- `kubectl logs` reads **one container**; specify `-c` in multi-container pods or it errors / picks the default.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl run logger -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 \
  --command -- sh -c 'echo MARKER=ckad-obs-42; sleep 3600'
kubectl logs logger -n ckad-observability            # read stdout
kubectl logs logger -n ckad-observability --previous # last crashed instance
kubectl create configmap captured -n ckad-observability \
  --from-literal=token=ckad-obs-42
kubectl -n ckad-observability get cm captured -o yaml
```

questions.title: Debug a running pod with an ephemeral container
questions.teach:
`kubectl debug` attaches an **ephemeral container** to a *running* pod — a temporary debug container sharing the pod's namespaces, so you can troubleshoot an image that has no shell/tools without restarting it. `--target=<container>` shares that container's process namespace.

**Gotcha:** ephemeral containers can't be removed or restarted — they're for live debugging, not permanent sidecars.
questions.prompt:
Pod `blackbox` in `ckad-observability` is running but you can't `exec` into its container `app`. Use `kubectl debug` to add an **ephemeral debug container** (image `busybox:1.36`) targeting container `app`.

Target: pod `blackbox` has an ephemeral container using image `busybox:1.36`.
questions.hint: `kubectl debug -it blackbox -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --target=app -- sh` — the ephemeral container stays recorded on the pod even after you exit.
questions.solution:
kubectl debug -it blackbox -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --target=app -- sh
# exit the shell; the ephemeral container remains on the pod
kubectl get pod blackbox -n ckad-observability -o jsonpath='{.spec.ephemeralContainers[*].image}'

verification.description: pod 'blackbox' has an ephemeral debug container (busybox:1.36)

questions.eli5:
Imagine a sealed submarine already underwater on a mission — you can't surface it or rebuild it without ruining the trip. Something inside looks off, but the submarine has **no windows and no tools** on board (the container image has no shell). How do you look around without aborting the dive?

You send in a tiny **diver** who swims into the *same* submarine, breathes the same air, and shares the same rooms. That diver is an **ephemeral container** — a temporary troubleshooting container you attach to a *running* pod with `kubectl debug`. It brings its own toolbox (the `busybox:1.36` image), so even though the original container is bare, you now have a shell and tools right next to it.

The `--target=app` part is the key: it tells the diver to swim into the **same room** as the `app` container — sharing its process view — so you can actually see and poke at `app`'s processes, not just float in an empty compartment.

The best part: you never had to resurface. The pod keeps running the whole time; no restart, no downtime.

**Watch out:**

- **Ephemeral containers can't be removed or restarted.** Once you attach the diver, it's a permanent entry in the pod's record — great for a live look, wrong for a long-term sidecar.
- **`--target=<container>` is what shares the target's process namespace.** Leave it off and your debug container can't see the target container's processes.
- It attaches to a **running** pod — if the pod has already crashed, you debug differently (e.g. `kubectl debug` creating a *copy*, or reading `--previous` logs).
- The debug container **shows up on the pod spec** even after you `exit` the shell — that's expected, and it's exactly what the check looks for (`ephemeralContainers[*].image` = `busybox:1.36`).
- It's an add-on, not a replacement: the original `app` container keeps running untouched.
questions.deepDive: ## Debugging a running pod with an ephemeral container ### Mental model An **ephemeral container** is a temporary container injected into an *already-running* pod. It shares the pod's network and (optionally, via `--target`) a chosen container's **process namespace**, so you get a shell and tools next to a container whose own image has none — **without restarting the pod**. It's added to `pod.spec.ephemeralContainers` and cannot be removed. ``` Running pod "blackbox" ├─ container: app (distroless/no shell — can't exec in) └─ ephemeralContainer: debugger ◀── kubectl debug --image=busybox:1.36 --target=app shares app's PID namespace → sees app's processes ``` ### The command ```bash kubectl debug -it blackbox -n ckad-observability \ --image=busybox:1.36 --target=app -- sh # exit the shell; the ephemeral container REMAINS recorded on the pod ``` Verify it was added: ```bash kubectl get pod blackbox -n ckad-observability \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.ephemeralContainers[*].image}'; echo # busybox:1.36 ``` ### Key flags of `kubectl debug` | Flag | Meaning | |---|---| | `-it` | interactive TTY (attach a shell) | | `--image=` | image for the debug container (brings the tools) | | `--target=` | **share that container's process namespace** (see its PIDs) | | `-c ` | name the ephemeral container (else auto-generated `debugger-xxxxx`) | | `--` *cmd* | command to run (e.g. `sh`) | > **Attach to a running pod** → ephemeral container (`--target` for shared PIDs). > Other `kubectl debug` modes (not this task): `--copy-to=` clones the pod with changes; `node/` debugs a node via a host-namespace pod. ### Why not just `exec`? `kubectl exec` needs a shell/binary **inside the target container**. Minimal images (distroless, scratch, `FROM nginx` stripped) have none, so `exec … sh` fails. Ephemeral containers bring their own userland alongside the target. ### How `--target` changes what you see | With `--target=app` | Without `--target` | |---|---| | Shares `app`'s **PID namespace** | Separate PID view | | `ps` shows `app`'s processes | only the debug container's processes | | Can inspect `/proc/` of `app` | cannot | (Requires the container runtime to support process-namespace sharing — true on standard kind/containerd.) ### Gotchas & exam traps - **Ephemeral containers can't be removed or restarted** — no `rm`, no `edit` to delete. They're for live, one-off debugging, **not** permanent sidecars. - They persist on the pod **after you exit the shell** — that's normal and is exactly what verification checks. - **`--target` is required to share the target's process namespace.** Omit it and you can't see the other container's processes. - Works on a **running** pod. For an already-crashed/completed pod, use `kubectl debug --copy-to` or read `kubectl logs --previous`. - You **cannot** add an ephemeral container by editing the pod with `kubectl edit`/`apply` — it goes through the special `ephemeralcontainers` subresource that `kubectl debug` uses. - The original `app` container is untouched; the debug container is additive. ### Quick reference ```bash # attach a debug container to a running pod, sharing app's PIDs kubectl debug -it blackbox -n ckad-observability \ --image=busybox:1.36 --target=app -- sh # confirm it's recorded on the pod kubectl get pod blackbox -n ckad-observability \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.ephemeralContainers[*].image}'; echo # busybox:1.36 kubectl describe pod blackbox -n ckad-observability | grep -A5 'Ephemeral Containers' ```
